# SK2033 — Do not stackalloc inside a loop

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `stackalloc` sits in a loop body, condition or incrementor, so the frame grows by one buffer per iteration and none of them is released until the method returns.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

Stack memory allocated in a method is reclaimed when that method returns, not when the block ends. A `stackalloc` a loop repeats therefore grows the frame by an amount the loop bound decides, and the overflow it eventually causes is a process kill with no catchable exception and no diagnostic naming this line. No fix is offered: hoisting the buffer out of the loop changes its lifetime and whether iterations share it, which is a decision about the program rather than a rewrite of it.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
for (var i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[64];
    Fill(buffer, i);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[64];
for (var i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    Fill(buffer, i); // after deciding the iterations may share one buffer
}
```

## When it does not fire

Purely syntactic: the enclosing `for`, `foreach`, `while` or `do` is found by walking outward and stopping at a lambda, an anonymous method, a local function or a member body, because a separate frame releases its own stack on return. Positions a loop evaluates only once are excluded — a `for` initializer or declaration, and a `foreach` source expression — while conditions and incrementors are reported, since a loop re-evaluates those. ⚠ A loop that cannot reach a second iteration is excluded and this is the judgement the rule makes deliberately: `do { … } while (false)`, `while (false)`, and a body whose direct statements include an unconditional `break`, `return` or `throw`. That last exclusion is withdrawn when the body contains a `continue` or a `goto` of its own, because either can reach the `stackalloc` again and the `break` then proves nothing. Conditional exits, loop bounds and recursion are not analysed; a loop whose body always exits through an `if` is still reported, because proving that needs the dataflow this rule does not do.
